title: What's Left When It Runs Out
logline: At a roadside free-food stall on a festival day, volunteers watch the queue grow longer than the food will stretch, and in a few seconds, again and again, someone has to decide how to share what is left.

object.note: Object 5 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject. Object 2, acquired with wanting, may also be present at the moment the series first turns toward giving.

thread_in.thread: Inside that fast, unowned process there is still room to choose, and the next film finds it at a roadside free-food stall where, again and again, someone decides how to share what is left.

thread_out.thread: In that gap, goodness can be chosen: from a festival stall's free food to a roadside family that has fed passing strangers for years and hands Chathura a plate before he asks.

requirements: A roadside dansala or free food stall during a real religious festival, with organisers willing to allow filming
A festival day where demand plausibly outpaces supply, without the film creating or worsening any real shortage
Consent from volunteers and, where practical and respectful, from those being served

suggestions.name: A town along the Kataragama pilgrimage route during a festival period
suggestions.why: The Kataragama pilgrimage route has a long tradition of roadside dansala hospitality during festival seasons.
suggestions.season_notes: Timing would need to align with an actual festival or poya period with heavy pilgrim traffic.
suggestions.access_notes: Organisers' cooperation would be essential and filming must never slow down or interfere with real service.
suggestions.verify: A specific stall, organisers, and a festival date with genuinely constrained supply are unconfirmed.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed.

lesson.in_simple_terms: Everything before a response, the seeing, taking in and sorting, runs the same way in everyone and carries no wish to act. The moment of response is where generosity, or its absence, takes shape, and this series treats that moment as a choice.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: දැකීම, පිළිගැනීම හා විමසීම සැමටම එක ලෙස සිදු වන අතර, දීමේ සිත හෝ නොදීමේ සිත, එනම් පින හෝ පව, හැඩ ගැසෙන්නේ ඉන් පසු එන ජවන් සිත්වලය.
lesson.the_teaching: The Abhidhamma names fourteen functions a mind-moment can perform, and places the doing of action, and of merit and demerit, in impulsion (javana): the few 'running' moments that follow once the object has been determined (C034). The rootless minds that come before it, seeing, receiving, investigating and determining, contain only ethically neutral factors and never the wish to act (chanda) (C029, C025). In the fullest process the impulsion is wholesome, unwholesome or merely functional (C041). The texts do not call this stage 'choice' and describe no separate chooser standing behind it; reading it as the moment a person chooses is the series' own interpretation.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The film watches the queue lengthen as supplies thin: portions held steady, then hesitation, smaller scoops and quick conferring among volunteers. Each new face at the front brings the same fast moment round again, and the different ways servers meet the same shortage let the viewer see where generosity is made, without anyone saying so.

key_terms.en: impulsion: the 'running' moments where action is made

lesson.caution: This is not the slogan 'the gap between stimulus and response is where your freedom lies': the texts describe impulsion as part of a process far too fast to feel, not as a conscious pause for weighing options.
lesson.builds_on: The bus driver showed a process no one arranges; this film finds, inside that same process, the stage where a response takes on its moral quality, and watches it happen again and again at a food stall.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
